_comment: The committed wall-clock budget of the sandboxes.
app_spec.xml, Untrusted Code Sandbox, feature 163:
System persists a timeout fail class after hard-killing a sandboxed
run that exceeded its 30 second wall clock budget
(docs/nullius-tech-architecture.md section 5.2: the one call site
passes limits=Limits(wall_s=30, cpu_s=30, mem_mb=2048,
network=False, filesystem=False, pids=32), and the control table's
own row is 'Timeout | Hard kill, recorded as fail_class=timeout';
section 9.1's node column is 'fail_class TEXT -- ok | timeout |
error | tripwire_fail'; section 8's ledger carries the same four as
'outcome TEXT NOT NULL'; section 6.1 step 11 writes the charge even
when the node fails, because 'a failed evaluation still consumed a
hypothesis').
The compile in packages/sandbox/src/sandbox/timeout.py refuses this
file and any change to it that does not declare the wall budget of 30
seconds - so the number below is not a convention the next edit can
forget: it is the law, checked, and a run dispatched past it is
hard-killed and recorded with the fail class 'timeout'.
Why 30 is written down at all, when the runner could default to it.
A budget is a claim about how long untrusted code may hold a core, and
a claim of that shape has to be reviewable: the same reason feature
157's isolation policy and feature 167's import allowlist ship as files
rather than as literals in a launcher. The number here is the one
section 5.2's call site passes and the feature's own sentence names,
and the compiler refuses any other - so 'this deployment kills at 30
seconds' is a fact about a file in the repository rather than a line in
a runbook.
One budget for every box the isolation policy covers, and deliberately
not a per-component block: section 5.2's table gives the isolation row
one mechanism per box because a box is what isolation is a property of,
while the wall budget is a property of the run and the call site passes
the same Limits to each of them. A per-component table here would be a
knob nobody turns.
cpu_s, mem_mb and pids are deliberately absent: they are the same
Limits(...) call's other three fields, and they belong to feature 162's
cgroup law. This file holds the one field feature 163's sentence is
about.
